passage:
Dear Chetan,
You asked how I'm holding up while the scholarship list is still not out. Honestly, the first week I refreshed the portal every hour and barely slept. Then Mausi made me write two columns on the back of an old calendar.
Left side: things I can move. I finished the fee-waiver form, emailed the hostel warden about a cheaper room, and fixed two tuition students for Saturday mornings. Right side: the committee's decision, the date, the number of seats. That column I read once a day and then leave alone.
It still itches, not knowing. But yesterday I went a whole evening without checking, and it felt like a muscle getting a little stronger.
Come over Sunday? I'll make chai.
Lokesh

qa.q: What did Lokesh put on the left side of the old calendar?
qa.a: Things Lokesh can move: the fee-waiver form, an email to the hostel warden about a cheaper room, and two tuition students for Saturday mornings.

qa.q: How was Lokesh feeling in the first week of waiting, and what shows it?
qa.a: Lokesh felt anxious and restless; refreshing the portal every hour and barely sleeping show how hard the not-knowing was.

qa.q: What turning point helped Lokesh stop checking the portal so often?
qa.a: Writing the two columns with Mausi let Lokesh act on the form, the room and the tuition, and choose to read the other column only once a day.

qa.q: If Chetan is waiting on something uncertain too, what might Chetan take from this letter?
qa.a: Chetan might feel less alone in the worry and pick up a simple way to sort what can be acted on from what has to be left for now.

grounding: Shows a young adult sorting what can be acted on from what cannot, planning the possible parts and growing better at tolerating not knowing.

passage:
So, Dilnaz, you know my little brother Sonu took the overnight train to Pune alone last month? I was a mess. I wanted to track every station, call him every hour, make him send photos of his berth.
Then around ten at night I caught myself and asked, okay, what can I actually do from here? I could make sure he had the charger, the uncle's number at the other end, and snacks. Done, all packed.
The train running late, who sits in his compartment, whether he sleeps, none of that was mine to hold. So I told him, one message when you board, one when you wake. Then I put my phone face-down and watched a film with Amma, who kept saying, 'See, Chandrika, the world hasn't ended.'
I still woke at four and checked. But less than I would have a year ago. It gets easier each time, honestly.

qa.q: What two messages did Chandrika ask Sonu to send?
qa.a: One message when he boards and one when he wakes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika afraid of at first, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Chandrika was worried about Sonu travelling alone; wanting to track every station and call every hour shows that fear.

qa.q: Which choice at ten at night changed how Chandrika handled the worry?
qa.a: Asking what could actually be done from home led Chandrika to pack the charger, the uncle's number and snacks, and then let go of the delays and the rest.

qa.q: How might Sonu have felt being asked for only two messages instead of hourly calls?
qa.a: Sonu probably felt trusted and less watched, free to enjoy his first solo trip while still knowing his family cared.

grounding: Shows a young adult planning for the parts of a relative's trip that can be influenced, letting go of the rest, and finding that not knowing gets easier with practice.

passage: I'm Lalit, and I've shared a hostel room with Harsha for two years, so I saw the whole of results week. Harsha had applied to three master's programmes and heard nothing. The old Harsha would have refreshed the inbox every ten minutes. This time I watched Harsha make a list on our whiteboard, in two columns. "Can do: finish the backup application, practise for interviews, sleep." "Can't do: make them reply faster." Then Harsha wiped the second column and went for a run. I don't know what was going on inside. Harsha still checked the phone at night; I saw that. But the backup form got sent on Wednesday, and on Thursday Harsha laughed at my terrible cooking.

qa.q: How many master's programmes had Harsha applied to?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling during results week?
qa.a: Harsha was probably anxious about the silence, still checking the phone at night, but calmer than before.

qa.q: What did Harsha do that helped with the uncertainty?
qa.a: Separated what could be done from what couldn't, acted on the first list and let go of the second.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the change in Harsha?
qa.a: Lalit notices a calmer roommate who acts and even laughs, while admitting not knowing Harsha's inner state.

grounding: Shows through a roommate's eyes a young adult separating what can be influenced from what cannot and tolerating not knowing.

passage:
Monday: Placement results were delayed again. Pallavi paced the hostel corridor, checking the portal twenty times, unable to eat. Her friend Jahnavi asked, "What can you actually do today?" Pallavi snapped, "Nothing. That's the problem."
Wednesday: Pallavi sat down with a notebook and split a page in two. Could change: polish the backup CV, apply to two small firms, call Mummy. Couldn't change: the company's timeline. She did the first three things and closed the portal.
The following Monday: Still no result. Pallavi noticed the tight feeling, named it, and went to badminton anyway. "Not knowing is awful," she told Jahnavi, "but I'm getting better at it."

qa.q: How many times did Pallavi check the portal on Monday?
qa.a: Twenty times.

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling on the first Monday?
qa.a: She was anxious and frustrated, unable to eat and snapping at Jahnavi.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Pallavi split what she could change from what she couldn't and acted on the first, which gave her some control and calm.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel hearing "I'm getting better at it"?
qa.a: Jahnavi likely feels glad and relieved that her question helped, even after being snapped at.

grounding: Shows over days a young adult learning to plan for what she can influence and let go of the rest while waiting.

passage: Kunal, you're checking that phone like it owes you money. Let me tell you something. When I was twenty-one, my father was in a Lucknow hospital for a heart operation, and I was two hundred kilometres away with final exams. I couldn't sleep. I rang the ward every hour until the sister there said, kindly, "Beta, we'll call you. Go and write your exam." That night I, Divyansh, made two lists on the back of a notebook. What I could do: study, call my mother each evening, take the Sunday bus. What I couldn't: the operation itself. I tore off the second list and put it in my pocket. I still worried. But I wrote the exams, and I was there on Sunday. My father's fine, by the way. Still grumbling.

qa.q: How far away was young Divyansh from the hospital?
qa.a: Two hundred kilometres away.

qa.q: What was young Divyansh feeling while ringing the ward every hour?
qa.a: Divyansh was frightened and restless, unable to sleep, desperate for news.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Making two lists after the nurse's words and tearing off the list of things Divyansh couldn't control.

qa.q: How might the nurse have felt getting a call every hour?
qa.a: The nurse was probably busy but sympathetic, understanding Divyansh's fear and gently sending Divyansh to the exam.

grounding: Shows a young adult separating what could be done from what couldn't during a parent's operation, and learning to tolerate not knowing.

passage:
Fog had grounded every flight out of Lucknow, and Sonali's interview for the Bengaluru fellowship was at ten the next morning. Around her, people shouted at the airline desk.
Her friend Nandini called. "What are you going to do?"
Sonali took out a notebook and drew a line down the middle. On one side: the fog, the airline, the panel's decision. On the other: emailing the panel, checking the overnight train, preparing her answers.
She emailed first, briefly and politely, asking about an online interview. She booked a train seat as a backup. Then she sat on her suitcase and practised her answers aloud.
"And if they say no?" Nandini asked.
"Then I'll have done what I could." Her stomach still fluttered, but her voice was calm.
At midnight, the reply came: online would be fine.

qa.q: What had grounded every flight out of Lucknow?
qa.a: Fog.

qa.q: How was Sonali feeling while she waited for the reply?
qa.a: She was still a little nervous, with her stomach fluttering, but calm enough to plan and practise.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that others in a similar situation could copy?
qa.a: She split the problem into what she could and couldn't influence, acted on the first by emailing, booking a backup train and practising, and let go of the rest.

qa.q: How might Nandini see Sonali's calm?
qa.a: Nandini, who asked "What if they say no?", may be surprised and reassured that Sonali can accept not knowing after doing what she could.

grounding: Shows a young adult separating what she can influence from what she cannot, planning for the possible and tolerating not knowing.
